title: SSD Controller Management
summary: The flash translation layer, garbage collection, and wear leveling that hide flash's erase-before-write quirks from every application on top.

slides.markdown:
The **flash translation layer (FTL)** is firmware inside the SSD controller that maps **logical block addresses** (what the OS thinks it's writing to) onto **physical flash locations** (wherever the controller actually put the data). This indirection is what hides flash's erase-before-write constraint ([ssd-and-flash-internals](ssd-and-flash-internals)) from the operating system entirely.

Without the FTL, every write would require the OS itself to track which physical pages are stale, which are free, and when to erase — flash would be nearly unusable as a generic block device. The FTL exists so an SSD can present the same simple "write any logical address" interface an HDD does.

**Write amplification** is the ratio between how much data the SSD physically writes internally versus how much data the host actually asked it to write. Because a logical overwrite becomes "write to a fresh page, mark old stale, eventually relocate survivors during garbage collection," one small logical write can trigger several extra physical writes.

A write amplification factor of 1.0 would mean perfect efficiency (no extra writes); real SSDs under sustained random-write load commonly see factors of **2–10x** or higher. Every extra physical write also consumes one of a flash cell's finite erase cycles — so write amplification directly eats into the drive's lifespan.

**Garbage collection (GC)** is how the controller reclaims blocks that have become a mix of **live** (still-valid) and **stale** (overwritten/deleted) pages. Since erasing works at block granularity, the controller must first **relocate** the still-live pages to a fresh block before it can erase the old one and return it to the free pool.

GC runs continuously in the background, and it's a direct source of write amplification: relocating live data means writing it again, purely for the controller's own bookkeeping — work the host never asked for and doesn't see directly, but pays for in reduced headroom for actual application writes.

Each flash cell can only survive a **finite number of erase cycles** before it becomes unreliable. If the same physical blocks were erased and rewritten far more often than others — as would happen if the FTL always reused the same "convenient" locations — those blocks would wear out and fail long before the rest of the drive.

**Wear leveling** is the FTL's strategy of spreading writes and erases evenly across all physical blocks, so no block bears a disproportionate share of the wear. Combined with GC's block relocation, this is also why even rarely-changing ("cold") data sometimes gets physically moved — to free up the block it occupies for wear-leveling purposes.

Watching one fragmented block get reclaimed makes the live/stale distinction and the relocate-then-erase sequence concrete.

![A fragmented flash block with live and stale pages; the controller relocates the live pages to a fresh block before erasing the original](assets/ssd-garbage-collection.svg)

Only after every live page has been safely copied elsewhere does the controller erase the original block — erasing before relocation would silently destroy still-valid data.

assets.alt: A fragmented flash block with live and stale pages; the controller relocates the live pages to a fresh block before erasing the original

slides.markdown:
Without extra information, the SSD controller has no way to know a logical block is "deleted" — file deletion happens in the filesystem layer, entirely above the FTL's view; from the drive's perspective, that data still looks live. **TRIM** is the command the OS sends to tell the SSD which logical blocks are no longer in use, so the controller can treat their physical pages as stale immediately.

Without TRIM, garbage collection would faithfully preserve and relocate data the filesystem already considers garbage — wasting GC effort and inflating write amplification for no benefit. TRIM is what lets the SSD's own notion of "stale" stay honest with the filesystem's.

A common mistake is estimating SSD lifespan or write-heavy workload performance using only the **host-visible** write volume — the bytes the application thinks it wrote. That number ignores everything the FTL does underneath: garbage collection's relocation writes, wear-leveling moves, and any internal metadata updates.

Under a sustained small-random-write workload with little free space (low over-provisioning), a real SSD's internal write volume can be several times the host's, meaning both **endurance** and **sustained throughput** can be far worse than a naive host-bytes calculation predicts. Accounting for write amplification — and giving the drive enough spare capacity to keep it low — is essential for realistic capacity planning.

slides.sectionTitle: Over-provisioning as a lever against write amplification
slides.subTitle: Reserving spare capacity the OS never sees
slides.markdown:
**Over-provisioning (OP)** reserves a slice of the drive's raw flash capacity that never appears in the advertised, OS-visible size — a 1TB-advertised drive might physically contain 1.1TB or more of flash. That spare capacity gives the garbage collector more free blocks to work with at any moment, which directly reduces write amplification: the FTL has more headroom to pick low-fragmentation victim blocks to erase, instead of being forced to reclaim heavily-fragmented ones under pressure.

This is precisely why datacenter and enterprise SSDs ship with far more over-provisioning (commonly 20-28% of raw capacity, sometimes more) than consumer drives (often just a few percent) — write-heavy server workloads need the garbage collector to have breathing room, and buyers explicitly trade usable capacity for lower write amplification and more predictable latency under sustained writes.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: turning fragmentation into write amplification
slides.subTitle: Why a nearly-full drive writes so much more than it's asked
slides.markdown:
Garbage collection reclaims a block that's 70% live, 30% stale. To free that block, the controller must first relocate every live page to a fresh block before erasing:

```
host asked to write:        1 page
GC relocates (per reclaim): 0.7 * block_pages  (all live pages in the victim block)

if a block holds 256 pages:
  live pages relocated per reclaimed block = 0.7 * 256 ~= 179 pages

write amplification factor ~= (1 host write + 179 relocated) / 1 host write
                            ~= effectively very high under heavy fragmentation
```

The key lever is that live fraction: reclaiming a block that's only 10% live relocates just ~26 pages instead of ~179 — nearly 7x less relocation work for the same one erase. This is exactly why keeping free space available (via over-provisioning, or TRIM keeping deleted data off the live list) lets the controller preferentially reclaim mostly-stale blocks, driving write amplification down without changing the workload at all.
